strengths: Identifies important and understudied problem: robustness of data valuation to utility changes, with two well-motivated realistic scenarios
Novel geometric framework via spatial signatures that elegantly unifies utility trade-off and multiple-valid-utility scenarios
Solid theoretical contributions including closed-form robustness metric R_p with O(n² log n) complexity and rigorous proofs
Thorough empirical validation within scope with careful experimental controls (aligned sampling, fixed learning context) demonstrating consistent agreement between rank correlation and R_p
Insightful analysis of why Banzhaf achieves higher robustness through collinearity, with formal correlation decomposition
Excellent presentation with clear motivation, intuitive visualizations, and comprehensive appendices; practical metric suitable for addition to existing pipelines
weaknesses: Severe restriction to K=2: closed-form R_p only applies to 2D utility spaces; for K>2 only Monte Carlo approximation available. This critically limits applicability to multi-objective scenarios (3+ criteria)
Limited to binary classification with linear-fractional utilities; excludes negative log-loss, multiclass, regression, and other utility forms despite first-order approximation validation
Narrow experimental scope: only 100 train/50 test samples with simple logistic regression; no real data valuation applications (cleaning, subset selection) demonstrating practical impact
No guidance on remedies when robustness is low or practical thresholds for acceptable robustness; unclear whether low R_p actually predicts failures in downstream tasks

Incomplete analysis of Banzhaf superiority: while Section 4 shows correlation with intermediate-j contributions, lacks structural explanation; assumes but doesn't validate that marginal contributions at different sizes are uncorrelated

Foundational insight somewhat expected (different utilities yield different rankings); elegant geometric formulation follows fairly directly from semivalue linearity without deep justification for this perspective
Limited connection to practical impact: no experiments showing robustness metric correlates with actual data selection/cleaning performance or end-task outcomes
Reproducibility concerns: no code mentioned, complex aligned sampling strategy, small datasets suggest sensitivity to experimental details

strengths: Identifies and clearly motivates an important under-explored problem in data valuation—demonstrated powerfully through Table 1 showing rank correlations from -0.47 to 0.99 across datasets
Novel geometric framework based on spatial signatures elegantly converts utility robustness to a geometric problem via semivalue linearity
Closed-form solution for R_p in K=2 case computable in O(n² log n) time, competitive with semivalue approximation cost
Comprehensive empirical validation showing R_p tracks rank correlations consistently across datasets and multiple correlation metrics
Insightful analysis (Section 4, Figure 4) explaining why Banzhaf achieves higher robustness through spatial signature collinearity
Extensive appendices with detailed proofs, experimental protocols, and additional results support reproducibility
weaknesses: Severely limited scope: restricted to binary classification with linear-fractional utilities; no multiclass, regression, or other utility types; acknowledged but deeply restrictive for practical adoption

Framework only provides closed-form solution for K=2 utilities—many realistic scenarios require K>2 (fairness + accuracy + robustness + efficiency); for K>2 must resort to Monte Carlo sampling without theoretical guarantees

Experimental design limitations: only 100 train/50 test samples (data valuation is most relevant at scale); single learning algorithm (logistic regression only—neural networks, trees, kernels untested); utilities tested lack natural preference ordering in practice

Lacks actionability: paper measures robustness but offers no guidance on improving it, no algorithm for utility selection, no recommendations for choosing base utilities, no connection established between measured robustness and downstream task performance

Weak theoretical foundations: Proposition 3.1 is straightforward application of semivalue linearity; no finite-sample analysis, convergence guarantees, or theory explaining why practitioners should care about R_p beyond rank correlation variability
Critical assumption (Section 4) that marginal contributions at different coalition sizes are uncorrelated is stated as 'mild' but never empirically verified on real data
No comparison with alternative robustness approaches (ensemble methods, Bayesian uncertainty quantification, robust optimization)
Artificial motivation for 'multiple-valid-utility scenario': assumes practitioners are indifferent between accuracy, F1, recall—in practice domain expertise typically dictates preference
No sensitivity analysis to key choices: learning algorithm hyperparameters, decision threshold calibration, dataset size effects, number of features
Missing validation on primary motivating example: LLM fine-tuning (helpfulness-harmlessness tradeoff) is introduced but experiments use only logistic regression on tabular datasets

strengths: Novel geometric framework: The spatial signature concept elegantly leverages semivalue linearity to embed data points such that utilities become linear functionals, providing genuine theoretical insight into data valuation robustness.

Well-motivated problem: Clear identification of two practical scenarios (utility trade-offs and multiple-valid-utilities) where robustness matters, with compelling empirical evidence (Table 1) showing rankings can flip dramatically between utilities.

Rigorous mathematical development: Solid theoretical contributions including Proposition 3.1 and its K≥2 extension, hyperplane arrangement analysis, and closed-form expressions for E[ρₚ] with O(n² log n) complexity.

Comprehensive experimental validation: Multiple datasets, semivalues, utilities, and rank correlation metrics with careful experimental controls (fixed learning context, aligned sampling, Gelman-Rubin convergence checks).

Insightful analysis: Section 4 decomposition explaining why Banzhaf achieves higher robustness by connecting semivalue weight profiles to marginal contribution correlations at different coalition sizes.
Practical utility: Robustness metric is computationally efficient as an add-on to existing data valuation pipelines, with clear geometric interpretation and principled normalization.
Clear presentation: Well-structured narrative with effective motivation, good figures (especially spatial signatures), and comprehensive appendices with full proofs and derivations.
weaknesses: Significant scope limitations: Analysis restricted to binary classification with linear-fractional utilities parameterized by λ and γ. Explicitly excludes multiclass classification, regression, and non-linear-fractional utilities (e.g., negative log-loss), severely limiting real-world applicability.

K > 2 utilities limitation: Closed-form derivation of E[ρₚ] only applies to K=2 (two base utilities). For K>2, must resort to Monte Carlo approximation. Many practical scenarios require balancing 3+ criteria (accuracy, fairness, interpretability, efficiency).

Incomplete approximation validation: First-order Taylor expansion of linear-fractional utilities empirically validated only on F1-score and Jaccard (Table 3, ~2% discordance). Testing on broader utility families and edge cases would strengthen claims. The 'mild assumption' about marginal contribution uncorrelation (Section B.7) is stated but not empirically validated.

Limited practical guidance: While identifying that low robustness is problematic, the paper provides insufficient guidance on: (1) what Rₚ values constitute concerning robustness, (2) how practitioners should respond to low robustness, (3) concrete decision rules for practitioners using this metric.

Experimental scale: Datasets are small (100 train, 50 test) due to computational constraints, limiting generalizability to modern large-scale datasets. Only logistic regression used as learning algorithm; results unclear for other model classes where marginal contributions behave differently.

Incomplete mechanistic understanding: Paper shows correlation between Kendall correlation and Rₚ but doesn't deeply explain root causes. Limited investigation of what fundamental dataset/semivalue properties drive robustness/fragility or when this problem actually arises in practice.

Missing downstream validation: No empirical study of whether ranking robustness predicts downstream task performance in data cleaning or subset selection applications. Motivating LLM example is compelling but hypothetical; no real case studies.

Insufficient treatment of K > 2: No roadmap or discussion of extending closed-form results or efficient exact algorithms to K > 2 utilities, which is relevant for practitioners with multiple competing objectives.

strengths: Well-motivated problem with compelling empirical evidence (Table 1) that semivalue rankings are sensitive to utility choice
Novel and elegant geometric framework based on spatial signatures that unifies utility trade-off and multiple-valid-utility scenarios
Theoretically principled robustness metric Rp with clear interpretation, closed-form O(n² log n) computation, and connections to rank correlations and top-k stability
Comprehensive empirical validation across 8+ datasets, multiple semivalues, regression/classification settings, and extensions to K > 2 utilities
Insightful analysis via Proposition 3.3 explaining why Banzhaf achieves higher robustness through alignment of marginal contributions
Rigorous experimental design with careful controls (fixed learning context, aligned sampling) and thorough appendices with detailed proofs
weaknesses: Limited scope of multiple-valid-utility scenario: restricted to linear-fractional metrics, excludes important utilities (negative log-loss, cross-entropy), covers only subset of multiclass metrics
Primarily diagnostic tool identifying when to distrust data valuation but providing no solutions—no prescriptive guidance on utility selection or aggregation when robustness is low
Cannot use framework prospectively (must compute expensive semivalue scores first) limiting practical utility for practitioners choosing utilities
Alignment assumption in Proposition 3.3 (independence of marginal contributions across sizes) empirically verified only on 2 datasets (BREAST, TITANIC), limiting generality
Limited novelty in finding Banzhaf more robust (already known from Wang & Jia 2023, Li & Yu 2023); deeper characterization of robustness-collinearity relationship incomplete
Computational cost with small subsampled datasets (100-300 training examples); unclear how results scale to realistic dataset sizes, and O(n² log n) cost is expensive after semivalue approximation
No actionable guidance on acceptable robustness thresholds in practice or concrete recommendations beyond 'choose Banzhaf or be cautious'
Incomplete handling of ties: acknowledged in Appendix B.4 but not addressed in main metric, and impact on Figure 3 results not analyzed

strengths: Addresses a genuine practical problem: Table 1 convincingly shows data valuations can yield contradictory rankings under different valid utilities (Kendall correlations as low as -0.47)
Elegant geometric framework: The spatial signature concept is clean and intuitive, mapping utilities to directions and providing geometric interpretation
Thorough empirical evaluation: Comprehensive experiments across datasets/semivalues with careful experimental controls (fixed learning context, aligned sampling)
Well-motivated problem statement: Two scenarios (utility trade-off, multiple-valid-utility) are practically relevant with clear real-world examples
Consistent experimental findings: Banzhaf's superior robustness observed across virtually all settings with theoretical explanation via alignment factors (Proposition 3.3)
weaknesses: Limited core novelty: Proposition 3.1 is a trivial application of semivalue linearity; Appendix B.2 proof simply expands ϕ(z; ω, Σα_k u_k) = Σα_k ϕ(z; ω, u_k). This is an observation, not a contribution

Robustness metric lacks principled design: (1) Why p swaps specifically? (2) π/4 normalization is geometrically motivated but doesn't ensure practical interpretability (3) Simple rank correlation achieves nearly identical results (Figure 3), undermining Rp's necessity (4) No evidence practitioners need Rp

Weak theory-practice connection: Paper diagnoses instability but provides no actionable solutions. If practitioner finds low Rp, what should they do? For multiple-valid-utility scenario, doesn't help systematically choose among valid utilities

Limited theoretical scope: Multiple-valid-utility analysis restricted to linear-fractional metrics; first-order Taylor approximation only empirically validated; Proposition 3.3 assumes Cov(Δ_j(u₁), Δ_k(u₂))=0 for j≠k, verified on only 2 datasets

Post-hoc explanation for Banzhaf: Collinearity explanation via alignment factors works backward from empirical observation; no intuition for why Banzhaf's weight structure naturally induces collinearity

Experimental design concerns: (1) Tiny datasets (n=100) unrepresentative of real scenarios where data valuation helps most (2) Aligned sampling is experimental artifact; practitioners independently estimate values (3) No scalability demonstration despite O(n² log n) claims (4) Arbitrary choices (p values, utility pairs)
Missing practical validation: No case studies, user studies, or evidence that computing Rp improves practitioner decisions. Metric serves as diagnosis without providing solutions

strengths: Well-motivated problem with compelling empirical evidence (Table 1) showing utility choice dramatically affects rankings
Elegant theoretical framework via spatial signatures (Proposition 3.1) providing geometric intuition for semivalue-utility relationship
Practical robustness metric Rp with closed-form O(n² log n) computation and clear interpretation
Rigorous experimental methodology: fixed learning context, aligned sampling, Gelman-Rubin convergence criterion
Comprehensive empirical validation across datasets and semivalues with agreement across multiple correlation metrics
Insightful Proposition 3.3 decomposing correlation into size-j alignment factors, explaining Banzhaf's robustness advantage
Thorough appendices with detailed proofs, implementation details, and extended experiments
Clear presentation with effective visualizations and well-motivated problem formulation
weaknesses: Limited scope: multiple-valid-utility scenario focuses on binary classification with linear-fractional utilities; regression utilities fall outside scope
Key assumption in Proposition 3.3 (cross-size independence) empirically verified only on 2/8 datasets; generality of decomposition could be stronger
Dataset scale limited to 100-300 training points due to computational constraints; results may not generalize to realistic larger datasets
Limited actionable guidance when robustness is low; identifies problem but offers few solutions for practitioners facing low Rp
Choice of p in robustness metric somewhat arbitrary (p ∈ {500,1000,1500}); limited guidance on selecting p in practice
Shallow mechanistic explanation for why Banzhaf weights lead to collinear signatures; geometric insight present but deeper understanding lacking
Computational cost prohibitive for large-scale settings despite Rp being O(n² log n)—semivalue computation dominates with O(n² log n) model trainings required
Connection to downstream ML performance (e.g., does low Rp predict poor data selection) not explored; unclear practical thresholds for acceptable Rp values
